business: Fraser Brothers Group, LLC (Fraser Brothers Insurance Agency / DeLaurier / Kennedy & Ward), Edison, NJ
opportunity: Opportunity #1: 24/7 intake and quote-request triage agent across the three agency brands (audit.md, 'Requests answered within the hour')

problem.summary: Every inbound lead path at this 17-person, three-brand agency is human-gated and weekday-only. Quote and contact requests arrive through embedded Agency Revolution web forms (separate personal and commercial form IDs) or by phone; there is no online booking, no instant quote and no chat widget, and the three offices close between 4:15 PM (Edison) and 5:00 PM (Belford). A request sent Friday evening is therefore not acknowledged until Monday, and because Edison, Belford (DeLaurier) and Tinton Falls (Kennedy & Ward) each run their own name, phone number and hours, a person must manually decide which office, brand and producer owns each lead. The agency also sells ~10 commercial niches plus life/health/Medicare, so a request cannot be routed until someone reads it and classifies the line of business. The audit prices the intake work at roughly 832-2,080 staff hours a year (0.4-1.0 intake role) at $28.69/hour loaded, i.e. about $23,868-$59,670 a year, plus lead decay that is not counted.

solution.design: A thin, founder-built intake service (Python/TypeScript + Postgres, containerised on a small cloud VM) that sits between Fraser Brothers' existing channels and its existing systems. It owns three inbound channels for the Edison pilot: (a) the Agency Revolution website form webhook, (b) the shared office service inbox, and (c) missed-call/voicemail capture on the Edison main line. Each contact is normalised into one lead record with the raw source payload retained, the line of business and niche classified (e.g. personal auto vs contractor vs restaurant), urgency and after-hours flag set, and a proposed owner (brand/office/producer) computed from a routing table the principal signs off on. The agent then runs a short, scripted clarification exchange by email and SMS (3-5 questions: insured name, address/town, effective or renewal date, current carrier, key drivers/property or business details) and offers a callback or meeting slot. Everything client-facing is a draft: the agent writes the reply plus the qualification summary into an approval queue where a licensed producer or CSR edits, approves and sends; nothing is quoted, bound or advised by the agent. A daily exception queue catches unclassifiable items, anything mentioning a claim or a coverage question, and anything where the model reports low confidence. All events (received, classified, drafted, approved, sent, outcome) are appended to an audit log with the approving user ID, which is the artefact the agency needs for E&O and for a future carrier vendor review. Voice (a live AI answering agent on the three main lines) is deliberately out of the pilot: the pilot proves form/email/SMS triage and the approval workflow first, and voice is added as a priced phase 2 once the routing rules and reply library are trusted.

solution.human_in_the_loop: A licensed producer or CSR approves every client-facing message, every quote-related commitment and every coverage statement, before it leaves. The agent may acknowledge receipt, ask scripted qualification questions and offer a callback slot, but it never states a price, never compares coverage, never binds or endorses a policy and never releases a certificate. Any message mentioning a claim, a coverage question, a cancellation or a complaint leaves the automated flow immediately and is routed to a person (claims go to the office during hours, or to the carrier's 24-hour line after hours, which the agency already publishes). Low-confidence classifications go to the exception queue rather than being guessed, and all approvals are logged with the approver's identity.

pilot.scope: Four weeks, Edison office, personal lines only (personal auto and homeowners). Channels: the personal and commercial Agency Revolution website forms, the Edison shared service inbox, and missed-call/voicemail capture on the Edison main line. The agent acknowledges every enquiry within minutes, runs the 3-5 question qualification, classifies line of business and urgency, proposes the owning brand/office/producer, offers a callback slot and places a drafted reply plus summary in the approval queue. No voice agent, no quotes, no AMS write-back, no certificates. A producer or CSR approves every outbound message.
pilot.weeks: 4 weeks of pilot after roughly 3-3.5 weeks of build (14-18 founder-days for phases 0-3); total ~7 weeks from kickoff to pilot report
success_metrics: Share of after-hours and weekend enquiries acknowledged within 15 minutes (target >=90% of eligible enquiries)
Time to first response, measured against the pre-pilot baseline (target: median under 15 minutes for acknowledgements, versus next-business-day baseline)
Classification accuracy (line of business, office/brand, urgency) against a producer-reviewed 50-lead sample (target >=85% line-of-business accuracy, 100% of claim mentions escalated)
Draft acceptance rate: share of agent drafts sent with edits of one sentence or less (target >=70%)
Zero unapproved client-facing messages, zero price quotes, zero coverage statements issued by the agent (target: zero)
Staff minutes per lead before vs during the pilot (target: 15-30% reduction in handling time on pilot leads)
Number of leads rescued after hours that would previously have waited (reported, not targeted)
pilot.baseline_method: Primary: export submission timestamps from the Agency Revolution forms and the first outbound reply timestamps from the shared inbox/Bridge call and message logs for the prior 8-12 weeks, and compute time-to-first-response by hour-of-day and day-of-week. If timestamps are incomplete, run a two-week shadow period before go-live in which the assigned CSR logs received-at and first-replied-at for every enquiry; that log becomes the baseline. Staff minutes per lead are measured by a short manual time log on the same two weeks.
pilot.exit_criteria: Pilot is a success (proceed to production) if, over the final two weeks: >=90% of eligible after-hours enquiries acknowledged within 15 minutes; >=85% line-of-business classification accuracy on the gold set; >=70% draft acceptance; no unapproved, quoted or advisory message and no unresolved compliance flag; and the principal confirms the workflow reduced rather than added staff effort. Either side may stop at the end of the pilot with no further commitment, and no setup fee is due unless the agency proceeds. The pilot is also voidable at the start if Agency Revolution will not enable a usable webhook and no agreed fallback exists.

suggested_pricing.pilot_fee: $2,500 fixed for the four-week Edison personal-lines pilot, paid up front (inference)
suggested_pricing.setup_fee: $4,500 one-time for production configuration across the three brands, crediting the pilot fee if the agency continues within 30 days (inference)
suggested_pricing.monthly_fee: $550 per month for the pilot configuration (Edison, personal lines, forms + email + SMS); $950 per month once all three brands and the after-hours voice agent are live (inference)
suggested_pricing.reasoning: Inference throughout, reasoned against published competitor prices and the audit's impact estimate. The audit values the intake work at $23,868-$59,670 a year, and the agency has no public revenue or lead-volume data, so pricing is set as a small fraction of the low-end value rather than a share of it: $550/month (~$6,600/yr) is about 28% of the low end and about 11% of the high end, leaving the agency most of the benefit. It is priced around the obvious substitutes: Ruby at $250/month for 50 receptionist minutes and $720 for 200, Awava at $397/month after a $1,997 setup, Smith.ai at $1.67-$2.00 per call plus a $150-$500 monthly base, and the incumbent Bridge uplift from $35 to a listed $65 per user (about $510/month across 17 staff, arithmetic on published per-user prices). What justifies sitting at the top of that band rather than at RingReady's $39 flat rate is the work those products do not do here: three brands with three routing rules, classification across personal lines and ~10 commercial niches, a licensed-approver queue with an audit trail, and a measured baseline. The $4,500 setup is roughly 2.25x Awava's $1,997 because the build is 14-18 founder-days for phases 0-3 rather than a self-serve configuration - that works out at roughly $250-$320 per founder-day, deliberately low, with the run rate carried by the monthly fee against running costs of about $32-$67/month - and it covers the two things the agency cannot buy off the shelf: the multi-brand routing matrix and the approval/audit workflow. The $2,500 pilot fee is about 1.25x Awava's setup fee, small enough for a principal to approve without procurement, and large enough to fund the three-plus weeks of build that precede the pilot; it is deliberately below the $4,500 setup so that the pilot is the low-risk entry point. If the agency insists on a lower monthly, the fallback is the same $550/month with the voice agent and the second and third brands priced as separate $200/month modules.

leverage.point: The agency already owns the intake surface: Agency Revolution forms on an FMG Suite site, with a documented path to have a webhook added to nominated forms at no published extra product cost - so the pilot does not require a website rebuild or a new form vendor, provided the destination question is answered.

Bridge already documents an AMS360 integration (Web Service API user, screen pop, activity export, notification service) and prices the whole platform per user, so the write-back problem has a vendor-supported route at production stage even though the pilot does not need it.

Published, very low infrastructure rates make the gross margin on a retainer high: Telnyx SMS at $0.004 per part plus carrier fee, voice from $0.0032/min, numbers at $1.00 each per month, DigitalOcean from $12/month, and Claude Haiku 5.5 at $0.10 per MTok input put total running cost in the $32-$67/month range against a $550-$950 retainer.

Self-hostable, permissively licensed components (Cal.diy under MIT, published for self-hosting) let the consultancy build a shared core without per-seat fees, and MIT terms leave room to reuse the same scheduler in later agency builds.

The pattern is repeatable: a multi-brand independent agency with ~40 carrier appointments, 17 staff, weekday-only hours and vendor-generated content is a common shape, so one working build becomes a template for other independent agencies in Middlesex and Monmouth counties (inference from audit.md/profile.json, not a measured market size).

Local presence: the consultancy is based in Milltown, adjacent to the Edison office, so discovery, approver training and on-site E&O conversations can be done in person - something the SaaS vendors selling into this account cannot offer (inference from the two towns, not a measured drive time).

edge_vs_competitors: Against RingReady ($39/month) and Ruby ($250-$1,725/month) the edge is not price, it is coverage of the channels this agency actually loses leads on: the embedded web forms, the shared inbox and the three separately branded phone lines, with one lead record that carries the owning brand, office and producer. Against Awava and Smith.ai the edge is the licensed-approver queue and an audit trail built for a New Jersey producer's licensing constraint (the agent may never quote, advise or bind), plus a measured baseline rather than a self-serve setup. Against Structurely/21X the edge is a fixed, published price instead of a quote-only platform fee, and against Bridge's upper tier (listed at $65 per user, marked 'Call For Pricing') the edge is per-enquiry qualification and drafting rather than per-call summarisation, at roughly the same monthly money as that uplift across 17 seats. Where it has no edge: brand recognition, 24/7 human fallback (Smith.ai, Ruby), polished self-serve onboarding (RingReady activates in minutes), SOC 2-grade security attestations that a one-founder side business cannot show, and the fact that the buyer may simply prefer to turn on a feature in a vendor he already pays. The realistic positioning is 'the integration and approval layer for the enquiry flow you already own', sold on local presence and a four-week measured pilot, not on being cheaper.

risks_compliance.issue: Unlicensed activity: New Jersey treats soliciting, negotiating or selling insurance as requiring a producer licence, a single act is enough, and employees who solicit or negotiate by telephone or computer on behalf of a producer must themselves be licensed - an AI agent that discusses coverage or quotes prices looks like exactly that.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: N.J.A.C. 11:17A-1.3 (who must be licensed; single act sufficient; no licensed producer may allow an unlicensed person to transact; subsection (e) covers employees communicating directly with the public by mail, fax, computer or telephone)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Hard-block price, coverage, binding and certificate language in the agent's output filters; only an identified licensed producer or CSR can release a client-facing message; the pilot scope excludes coverage questions and routes any such message to a person; agency's E&O contact reviews scripts before go-live.

risks_compliance.issue: TCPA exposure if the agent makes AI-voiced calls without consent; the FCC has declared that the TCPA's 'artificial or prerecorded voice' prohibition encompasses current AI technologies that generate human voices, so such calls require prior express consent absent an exemption.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: FCC Declaratory Ruling FCC 24-17, CG Docket No. 23-362, 'Implications of Artificial Intelligence Technologies on Protecting Consumers from Unwanted Robocalls and Robotexts' (adopted Feb 2, 2024, released Feb 8, 2024)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Inbound-only voice in phase 2 (no outbound AI calling); SMS only as a reply to an inbound enquiry or with consent language on the form; honour STOP/HELP; no AI voice on marketing campaigns.

risks_compliance.issue: Application-to-person SMS on US 10-digit local numbers requires 10DLC brand and campaign registration before messages can be sent; the campaign registration includes a 'Message Flow' description of how users opt in.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Telnyx 10DLC documentation ('If your business is sending outbound text messages using 10-digit long code (10DLC) Local phone numbers in the US, you're required to register for 10DLC'; campaign fields include use case and message flow)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Register the agency's brand and a conversational/low-volume campaign (with the site's opt-in wording documented) before the pilot starts; budget the one-time brand and campaign fees, the recurring campaign fee, and allow lead time for review.

risks_compliance.issue: Data-security obligations for customer information: if the agency is a covered financial institution, nonpublic personal information handled by the agent and by the consultancy as a service provider must sit inside a written information security programme with designated accountability, encryption, MFA, service-provider oversight and incident response. INFERENCE, not stated by the cited page: the FTC guide's list of financial-institution examples does not name insurance agencies, so whether Fraser Brothers is covered depends on its activities and on which regulator has GLBA authority over it - to be confirmed with the principal or counsel.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: FTC Safeguards Rule, 16 CFR Part 314: written information security program, Qualified Individual, risk assessment, access controls, encryption, MFA, service-provider oversight, incident response (per the FTC's small-entity compliance guide)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Deliver a service-provider addendum either way: encryption at rest and in transit, MFA on all admin access, least-privilege and role-based access, no training on client data, defined retention and deletion, incident notification, and support for the agency's annual WISP review.

risks_compliance.issue: Call recording consent: New Jersey is a one-party-consent state, but the agency's callers may be in two-party-consent states, and recording an AI-handled call without notice is a needless risk.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-4(d) (interception by a party, or with one party's prior consent, is not unlawful unless used to commit a criminal, tortious or other injurious act)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Disclose recording/AI answering in the greeting, or disable recording and keep transcripts only; state the disclosure in the pilot scope and get E&O sign-off. Phase 2 only.

risks_compliance.issue: Regulatory expectations for AI in insurance are set at the insurer level; the insurer's own AI program must cover AI systems it uses even where a third-party vendor supplies them, so the agency's carriers may push vendor due-diligence and documentation requirements down onto the agency (that downstream pressure is an inference - the bulletin is addressed to insurers).
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: NJ DOBI Bulletin No. 25-03, 'The Use of Artificial Intelligence Systems in Insurance' (addressed to 'ALL INSURERS AUTHORIZED OR ADMITTED IN NEW JERSEY'), requiring a written AIS Program whose scope covers AI systems 'whether developed by the insurer or a third-party vendor'
risks_compliance.mitigation: Offer the agency a one-page system description, data-flow diagram, model/prompt version log and test results to hand to carriers; expect this to be requested at some point and price the documentation into the setup fee.

risks_compliance.issue: New Jersey Data Privacy Act obligations: the law only applies to controllers processing personal data of at least 100,000 consumers (or 25,000 consumers while earning revenue from selling personal data), and it expressly does not apply to a financial institution subject to GLBA Title V or an insurance institution subject to P.L.1985, c.179 - so it is unlikely to bind an agency of this size (inference).
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: P.L.2023, c.266 (N.J.S.A. 56:8-166.4 et seq.), section 2 applicability thresholds and section 10 exemptions (b) GLBA financial institutions and (d) insurance institutions subject to C.17:23A-1 et seq.
risks_compliance.mitigation: Handle the underlying insurance-privacy obligations as the operative regime (not reviewed here), and in any case honour access/deletion requests, minimise retained fields, and publish the SMS opt-in and privacy language on the form - which the 10DLC campaign also requires.

risks_compliance.issue: Errors-and-omissions exposure from a wrong classification or a drafted line that reads like advice, especially where life/health or Medicare enquiries carry medical detail.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: General professional liability exposure for producers; NJ DOBI Bulletin 25-03 emphasis on unfair trade practices and consumer harm, and N.J.A.C. 11:17A-1.3 on licensed activity (no E&O policy or carrier requirement is publicly documented)
risks_compliance.mitigation: Scope the pilot to personal auto/home; exclude medical details from the pilot data model; approver must edit or reject rather than rubber-stamp; full audit log; escalate anything involving claims, cancellations or coverage to a person. The agency should confirm its E&O carrier's position on AI-assisted intake - not confirmable from public sources.

risks_compliance.issue: Integration-dependency risk: the Agency Revolution webhook is added by the vendor's support team on request, only the AgencyZoom-destination use case is documented, and Bridge API access is gated behind a Custom plan with a 20-user minimum.
risks_compliance.rule_or_source: Agency Revolution documentation states the webhook is requested through its customer experience team and added by them to specified forms; Bridge pricing lists API access only on the Custom plan with a '20 User Minimum for Customization'
risks_compliance.mitigation: Make the pilot contract conditional on a usable webhook or an agreed alternative intake path (for example parsing the form notification emails the site already sends); do not promise AMS write-back until the agency's AMS and Bridge plan are confirmed.

feasibility.weeks_to_pilot: About 3-3.5 weeks of build (14-18 founder-days for phases 0-3) to a working Edison pilot, then a 4-week measured pilot; ~7 weeks kickoff to pilot report. Voice adds 2-3 weeks afterwards.
feasibility.reasoning: Technically this is a tractable build: the channels mostly exist and are documented (Agency Revolution adds webhook keys to nominated Forge forms on request, Bridge documents its AMS360 integration, Telnyx and Anthropic publish pay-as-you-go rates, self-hosted Cal.diy covers scheduling), the expensive part is rules and wording, not infrastructure, and running costs land at roughly $32-$67 a month. The conditions are concrete. First, the pilot must be sold as forms + inbox + missed-call capture with a licensed-approver queue - not as a live AI phone agent - because producer licensing (N.J.A.C. 11:17A-1.3, including its direct-communication clause) and the FCC's AI-voice ruling make voice the riskiest surface, and the agency has to trust the routing rules first. Second, it depends on two gates outside our control: Agency Revolution enabling a webhook whose destination we can actually use (documented only for the AgencyZoom destination), and knowing which AMS holds the book, because Bridge's documented AMS360 path only helps if they are on AMS360 and third-party write-back is not documented at all. Third, the commercial case is thinner than the technical one: the buyer is a single principal with no public revenue, lead volume or response-time data, the price floor is set by $39/month AI receptionists and $397/month agency packages with a $1,997 setup, and the incumbent Bridge vendor can add call intelligence for a per-user uplift. That is why the pilot is priced at $2,500 with a written baseline and explicit exit criteria: it buys the missing data (volume, after-hours share, time-to-response, draft acceptance) at low cost to both sides, and the outcome is a defensible either/or rather than an open-ended build.

discovery_questions: Which agency management system holds the book (AMS360, Applied Epic, HawkSoft, EZLynx, other), and is Bridge your phone system, your CRM, or just the secure-upload and texting tool?
Who administers your Agency Revolution/FMG website, and has Agency Revolution ever added a webhook to your forms - and can that webhook post to an endpoint we control rather than AgencyZoom?
Roughly how many quote requests, contact-form submissions and inbound calls do you get in a typical week, and how many arrive outside office hours or at weekends?
Do you currently measure time-to-first-response? If so, where does that timestamp live, and can we export 8-12 weeks of it?
Who decides which of the three brands, offices and producers owns a new enquiry today, and what are those rules written down as?
Do you text clients today from a business number, and does the website form carry opt-in language we can use for 10DLC registration?
Which calendar do producers actually use for callbacks, and do you want customers to self-book or only to request a slot?
What do your carriers give you as written appetite or underwriting guides, and who signs off on what the agent is allowed to say about eligibility?
What has your E&O carrier or broker said about AI-assisted intake, retention and call recording, and who signs off internally on scripts?
If the pilot works, who operates the approval queue day to day, what is the acceptable turnaround for approvals outside office hours, and what would make you switch it off?
caveats: Every business fact about Fraser Brothers comes from audit.md, profile.json and analysis.json and was treated as already sourced. When re-checked in this round, the site's /contact and /claims-center pages returned only Agency Revolution footer and copyright text, so office hours (Edison 8:15-4:15, Belford 5:00 close, Tinton Falls 4:30), the phone/fax lines and the 'call the office during business hours' claims guidance could not be re-verified from a page a verifier can open; they should be confirmed with the principal in discovery or against a retrievable source such as a Google Business Profile.

The audit's $23,868-$59,670 annual impact is an estimate built on NJ median wages and an assumed 0.4-1.0 FTE of intake work; no call volume, lead count, close rate or revenue figure for the agency is public, so no revenue or conversion claim is made anywhere in this plan.

Running costs assume a small pilot volume (roughly 600 enquiries, 1,500 SMS parts and 200-400 voicemail minutes a month, one Telnyx number). These volumes are inferences, not the agency's numbers, and the SMS, model and 10DLC lines will move with actual volume and the use case declared at registration.

Pilot fee, setup fee, monthly fee, founder-days and the 1.25x benefits loading are the consultancy's own inferences, not market prices; competitor prices are quoted as published and may change or be superseded by plan changes.
Vendor pages describing AI receptionist results (for example RingReady's '40% More Quotes') are vendor marketing claims and are treated as Low strength; they are not relied on for any figure here.
The design deliberately excludes live AI voice answering from the pilot; the feasibility and pricing reflect that narrower scope, and the voice phase would need its own compliance review.
Whether Bridge API write-back is available to this agency depends on their Bridge plan and their AMS, neither of which is public; the pilot does not depend on write-back.

The Safeguards Rule discussion applies the rule's content (which the FTC page confirms) to this agency as an inference; the cited FTC page does not state that insurance agencies are financial institutions.
data_gaps: No call, form or email volume data, and no measured time-to-first-response, are public: the baseline has to be built during discovery, and the pilot's value case rests on that measurement.
The agency's agency management system is unknown (Bridge documents AMS360, but the agency could be on Applied Epic, HawkSoft or EZLynx).

Which Agency Revolution form product the site uses (Forge website forms vs Fuse campaign forms) could not be determined from public pages, and the only webhook documentation I could open covers Forge website forms with an AgencyZoom destination; no Agency Revolution page confirming a Zapier or CSV export path - or a webhook to an arbitrary endpoint - was found in this session.
Whether Agency Revolution will point a webhook at a non-AgencyZoom endpoint is unconfirmed and must be settled in discovery; the pilot contract is conditional on it or on an agreed alternative.

Bridge's Custom plan (the only tier listing API access) is price-on-request with a 20-user minimum, so incremental API cost is not public, and no page I opened documents a third party writing into Bridge or AMS360.
Twilio's US voice and SMS rate tables were not read from the official pricing pages in this session, so Telnyx's published rates are used throughout; Twilio retail rates were not verified.
The office email platform (Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace) is not visible publicly, so that integration is marked unconfirmed.

Taxes, regulatory recovery and other carrier-level surcharges on Telnyx traffic were not quantified; the number rental and emergency-calling fees are now included in the running-cost table but per-message surcharges are not.

No customer reviews, ratings, job postings, headcount, revenue or premium figures could be retrieved (review and job sites blocked automated access), so the size of the intake pain is inferred from operating choices only.

Whether Fraser Brothers' carriers impose vendor due-diligence or AI documentation requirements on producers is not public; NJ DOBI Bulletin 25-03 is addressed to insurers, so any downstream agency obligation is an inference.

No New Jersey guidance specifically governing producer (as opposed to insurer) use of AI was found; the producer-side constraint that is actually confirmed is the licensing rule in N.J.A.C. 11:17A-1.3, plus E&O considerations that are not publicly documented.

N.J.S.A. 17:23A-1 et seq. (the insurance information privacy law referenced in the NJDPA exemption) was cited from the NJDPA text but its own requirements were not reviewed, so the agency's operative privacy obligations are unconfirmed.
Gross margins assume the consultancy does the build itself on its own tooling; no cost for founder time, insurance or business registration is included.
